name: Teufelberger 10mm Sirius Loop with Pinto Pulley
title: Teufelberger Sirius Loop with Pinto Pulley (10mm)
h1: Teufelberger Sirius Loop, 10mm, with Pinto Pulley
meta: Teufelberger Sirius loop in 10mm hitch cord paired with a DMM Pinto pulley: a ready-made hitch and tending pulley setup for MRS and SRS tree climbing.
tagline: A 10mm hitch cord loop matched with a Pinto pulley for a clean, self-tending hitch.
summary: The Teufelberger Sirius loop is a 10mm sewn hitch cord loop sold here bundled with a DMM Pinto pulley, so you get the hitch and the tending pulley in one order. It suits climbers building a Distel, VT or similar hitch on a moving or stationary rope system.
highlights: 10mm hitch cord loop from Teufelberger
Bundled with a DMM Pinto pulley for hitch tending
Works on MRS and SRS hitch-based systems
Pre-made loop, no knots to tie in the cord
Check compatibility with your climbing line diameter

body.h: How the setup works on the climb
p: A loop of hitch cord tied around the climbing line with a pulley below it is the backbone of most modern hitch-climbing systems. The pulley keeps the hitch dressed and lets you tend slack with one hand, so you can advance on a long limb walk or a straight trunk ascent without stopping to push the hitch up.

The Pinto has two separate attachment holes, which lets you clip the hitch loop and the rope bridge or bridge ring to different points and keeps everything lined up. Many climbers like it on a rope-tending setup because the sheave sits right under the hitch.
Buying the loop and pulley together saves matching parts later and gives you a known starting point. It is a good way to set up a second system or replace a worn one in one go.

Hitch cord grab depends on the cord, the climbing line and the hitch you tie. Test the combination close to the ground before you trust it aloft, and adjust the number of wraps or braids until it grabs reliably and releases smoothly.

Hitch cord is a wear item. Inspect it before every climb for glazing, stiffness, cuts or cover damage and retire it early. As with all life-support gear, use it within the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice, and get trained on the system. See more cords in our hitch cord and split tails range.

faq.q: What hitches can I tie with a 10mm loop?
faq.a: Common choices are the Distel, VT and Schwabisch. The right one depends on your climbing line, so test grab and release low to the ground first.

faq.q: Can I use the Pinto pulley for other jobs?
faq.a: Yes. It is a common hitch-tending pulley and also gets used for small redirects or a mechanical advantage setup, within its rated use.

name: Teufelberger multiSLING
title: Teufelberger multiSLING Adjustable Climbing Sling
meta: Teufelberger multiSLING is an adjustable sling for tree climbing anchors and gear attachment. Set the length to the stem, then inspect and retire on schedule.
tagline: An adjustable sling for anchors and attachment points that changes length to fit the tree.
summary: The Teufelberger multiSLING is an adjustable sling that lets you set an anchor or attachment point at the length the stem or limb calls for, instead of carrying a pile of fixed slings. Climbers use it for canopy and basal anchors, redirects and quick attachment points.
highlights: Adjustable length to suit different stem sizes
Useful for anchors, redirects and gear attachment
Fewer fixed-length slings on the saddle
Made by Teufelberger, a long-time arborist rope maker
Inspect before each use like any life-support textile

p: Fixed slings are simple, but the length is never quite right. A sling that is too long leaves a ring or carabiner hanging where it can load across an edge, and one that is too short won't reach around the stem. An adjustable sling lets you choke or basket the anchor and snug it so the hardware sits where you want it.

On an SRS climb that means a cleaner canopy anchor, and on the ground it makes a quick basal tie-off or a redirect without digging for the right length. It also cuts down on the number of slings hanging off your saddle.
It is also a handy piece for setting a temporary lanyard anchor or a gear hang point while you work a big lead, so it earns its spot on the saddle.

Follow Teufelberger's instructions for how the multiSLING may be configured and loaded, and do not improvise attachment methods it is not designed for. Keep the sling away from saw chains, sharp bark edges and chemicals such as bar oil and fuel.

Check the textile and any hardware for cuts, abrasion, heat glazing and deformation before every use, and retire it when in doubt. Anchors are life support, so set them under ANSI Z133 practice and only after proper training. Browse related cords and slings in hitch cord and split tails.

faq.q: Is the multiSLING a friction saver?
faq.a: No. It is an adjustable sling. Some climbers pair a sling with rings or a pulley to build a cambium saver, but the multiSLING itself is a sling.

faq.q: Can I use it for rigging loads?
faq.a: Use it only for the purposes and loads stated in Teufelberger's instructions. Rigging slings for heavy wood are usually a separate, rigging-rated product.

name: Yale Beeline 10mm Prusik Loop with Steel Ring
title: Yale Beeline Prusik Loop with Steel Ring, 10mm
h1: Yale Beeline Prusik Loop with Steel Ring, 10mm
meta: Yale Beeline prusik loop in 10mm with a steel ring, for friction savers, adjustable anchors and backup hitches. Beeline hitch cord grabs well and runs smooth.
tagline: A 10mm Beeline cord loop with a steel ring for anchors, friction savers and hitches.
summary: The Yale Beeline prusik loop is a 10mm loop of Beeline hitch cord fitted with a steel ring. Climbers use it to build adjustable friction savers and anchors, as a backup hitch, or to grab a line when rigging small pieces.
highlights: 10mm Yale Beeline hitch cord
Steel ring on the loop
Handy for adjustable friction savers and anchors
Beeline is a popular hitch cord for its grab and heat resistance
Inspect before each use and retire when worn

p: A loop with a ring is a small piece that solves a lot of problems. Tied as a prusik around a sling or a second rope, it makes an adjustable anchor point. Paired with a larger ring on a sling, it becomes part of a friction saver that protects the cambium and makes retrieval easier.

On the ground, a prusik loop with a ring is a quick grab on a lowering line or a way to hang a pulley for a small redirect. The steel ring gives a durable, smooth attachment that takes wear from rope and carabiners.
Because the loop is pre-made, you skip tying and dressing a double fisherman's, and the finished loop stays a consistent length for a repeatable setup every time you rebuild your saver or anchor.
Beeline is built as a hitch cord, so it grips well on common climbing lines and holds up to heat. Still, every hitch depends on the line it is tied to, so test any new combination low to the ground.

Inspect the cord and stitching before each use for glazing, flat spots and cuts, and check the ring for grooves or burrs. Use it only within Yale's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice, and get trained before relying on it for life support. More options are in our hitch cord and split tails section.

faq.q: Steel or aluminum ring?
faq.a: Steel is heavier but stands up better to rope wear, which matters on a ring that sees a lot of running rope.

faq.q: Can I tie a climbing hitch with this loop?
faq.a: It can be used for a prusik-style backup or anchor hitch. For your main climbing hitch, most climbers use an eye-and-eye or split tail sized for their system.

name: Teufelberger BSB White Split Tail with Tight Eye
title: Teufelberger BSB Split Tail, White, with Tight Eye
h1: Teufelberger BSB Split Tail, White, with Tight Eye
meta: Teufelberger BSB split tail in white hitch cord with a tight sewn eye for a neat climbing hitch. A practical replacement tail for your MRS or SRS hitch system.
tagline: A white hitch cord split tail with a tight sewn eye for a tidy, compact hitch.
summary: The Teufelberger BSB split tail uses white hitch cord with a tight sewn eye on one end, made to tie a compact climbing hitch on your line. Climbers who replace tails often like a pre-sewn eye because it clips cleanly to a carabiner and keeps the hitch short.
highlights: Teufelberger BSB hitch cord in white
Tight sewn eye clips neatly to a carabiner
Keeps the hitch compact and close to the pulley
Easy to spot on the line
Retire on wear, not on the calendar

p: A split tail is the short length of hitch cord that forms your climbing hitch, with one end clipped to the saddle carabiner and the other tied off. A tight eye sewn on one end takes the place of a knot. It sits snug on the carabiner gate and does not roll, which keeps the hitch short and easier to tend.
A shorter hitch means less slack to pull and a quicker advance, especially when you are tending with a pulley below the hitch.
White cord also makes it easy to see the hitch against bark and a dark climbing line, which helps when you are checking the hitch from a distance or teaching a newer climber what to look for.

Tie the hitch your system calls for, often a Distel or Valdotain tresse, then finish the tail with a stopper knot that you can check at a glance. Test the hitch close to the ground on your actual climbing line and adjust wraps until it grabs and releases well.

Hitch cord takes heat and abrasion every climb. Check for glazing, stiffness, cover damage and wear near the eye before each climb, and replace it early. Use it within the maker's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice, and get trained on hitch climbing. Compare other cords in hitch cord and split tails.

faq.q: How long should a split tail be?
faq.a: It depends on the hitch and how you finish it. Many climbers check the length needed for their hitch and stopper and buy to match.

faq.q: When should I replace a split tail?
faq.a: Replace it as soon as it shows glazing, stiffness, cuts or cover wear, and do not wait for a set schedule if you climb daily.

name: Yale 10mm Black Beeline Split Tail
title: Yale Beeline Split Tail, 10mm Black
meta: Yale Beeline split tail in 10mm black hitch cord with a sewn eye. A popular climbing hitch cord for grab and heat resistance on MRS and SRS tree climbing lines.
tagline: Black 10mm Beeline hitch cord with a sewn eye for your climbing hitch.
summary: The Yale Beeline split tail is a 10mm length of black Beeline hitch cord with a sewn eye, made to tie the friction hitch on your climbing line. Beeline is a go-to hitch cord for many climbers because it grips well, runs smoothly and handles heat.
highlights: 10mm Yale Beeline hitch cord
Black color
Sewn eye for clean carabiner attachment
Good grab and heat resistance
Fits common 11–13mm climbing lines, test first

p: Your hitch is the piece of gear you touch most on every climb. A split tail with a sewn eye clips to the saddle carabiner and takes the place of a tied knot, which keeps the hitch short and easy to tend. Beeline holds a hitch firmly under load and releases without much fight, which makes descending smoother.
Black cord shows less dirt and pitch staining than lighter colors, but that also means it can hide wear, so give it a close look.

A sewn eye also removes one knot from your inspection list. You still check the stopper knot on the tail end every climb, but the carabiner end stays the same length and shape every time you rebuild the hitch.

10mm Beeline is commonly paired with climbing lines in the 11 to 13mm range, but grab varies with the rope's cover and age. Test any new tail on your line close to the ground and adjust the wraps until it works.

Before each climb, check for glazing, stiff spots, cuts and wear near the sewn eye, and retire it early. Use it within Yale's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice, and get trained on hitch climbing before relying on it. Shop other options in hitch cord and split tails.

faq.q: Will 10mm Beeline work on my 11.7mm rope?
faq.a: It is a common pairing, but test it on your actual rope low to the ground and adjust the hitch before climbing.

faq.q: Does color matter?
faq.a: Only for visibility and preference. Black hides dirt but can also hide wear, so inspect closely.

name: CMI Micro Hitch Tending Pulley
title: CMI Micro Pulley for Hitch Tending
h1: CMI Micro Pulley for Hitch Tending
meta: CMI micro pulley sized for hitch tending on a tree climbing system. It keeps the hitch dressed and slack moving so ascents and limb walks go smoother.
tagline: A small pulley that sits under your hitch and keeps slack moving as you climb.
summary: The CMI micro pulley is a compact pulley for hitch tending, placed under your climbing hitch so you can pull slack through with one hand. CMI is a US maker of rope rescue and climbing hardware, and this pulley is sized for arborist hitch systems.
highlights: Compact pulley for hitch tending
Helps keep the hitch dressed and moving
One-hand slack tending on ascent
Made by CMI, a US hardware maker
Check sheave and rope fit before use

body.h: What a hitch tending pulley does
p: In a hitch-based climbing system, the pulley sits between the hitch and the rope tail, clipped to the same bridge or carabiner. When you pull the tail, the pulley pushes the hitch up the line, so slack comes in with one hand and the hitch stays dressed.
That makes a big difference on a long ascent or when you are walking out a limb and need to keep slack tight. A small pulley keeps the setup short so you lose less height each time you advance.

A compact pulley also has less to snag on as you move through the canopy. On a busy saddle with a top-handle saw, hand saw and lanyard, small hardware keeps the front of the bridge clean and easy to work with, which matters most when you are tending slack hand over hand on a long ascent.
Make sure the pulley fits the rope diameter you climb on and the carabiner you use to connect it. Check that the side plates open and close properly and that the sheave spins freely.

Inspect for grooves, cracks, deformation and stiff bearings before each climb, and retire it if anything looks off. Use it within CMI's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice, and get trained on your climbing system. See more in micro pulleys.

faq.q: Can I use a micro pulley for rigging?
faq.a: Only within its rated loads and the maker's instructions. Rigging usually calls for a larger pulley built for those forces.

faq.q: Does the pulley work with any hitch?
faq.a: It works with most hitch systems that use a tending pulley. Check that your hitch length and carabiner fit it well.

name: CMI Shackle Pulley
title: CMI Shackle Pulley: Compact Pulley with Shackle
meta: CMI shackle pulley with a built-in shackle attachment, used for redirects, hitch tending and light mechanical advantage. Compact US-made hardware for tree work.
tagline: A compact pulley with an attached shackle for quick redirects and light hauling.
summary: The CMI shackle pulley pairs a pulley with an attached shackle, so you can connect it to a sling or anchor without a separate carabiner. Arborists use it for redirects, small mechanical advantage setups and hitch tending where a clean attachment helps.
highlights: Pulley with attached shackle
Clean connection to slings and anchors
Handy for redirects and light haul systems
Compact for the saddle or gear bag
Inspect sheave, axle and shackle pin before use

p: A shackle pulley lets you hang a pulley straight from a sling, ring or eye without stacking another carabiner, which keeps the system short and reduces cross-loading risk. That is useful for a quick redirect on a climbing line or for building a small mechanical advantage to tension a line.
Because the shackle stays with the pulley, it is one less piece to find when you set up. Keep it on a gear loop where you can reach it.

The shackle style also suits fixed points such as an eye on a sling, a ring on a friction saver or a tie-in on the truck. Keep in mind that a shackle takes a moment longer to open than a carabiner, so it fits best where the pulley stays put for the whole job rather than being moved every few minutes. For quick, frequent moves, many climbers still carry a carabiner pulley as well.

Check that the shackle pin threads fully and stays secure, that the sheave spins freely and that the side plates are not bent. Look for grooves where rope runs and replace the pulley if it shows cracks or deformation.
Use it within CMI's rated loads and instructions. Any part of a life-support system must be used under ANSI Z133 practice and by trained climbers. Compare it with other models in micro pulleys.

faq.q: Do I still need a carabiner?
faq.a: Often not. The shackle connects directly to a sling or eye, but follow CMI's instructions for approved connections.

faq.q: Is it suitable for heavy rigging?
faq.a: No. It is a compact pulley. Heavy rigging calls for a rigging block rated for those loads.

name: DMM Pinto Pulley Spacer
title: DMM Pinto Spacer for the Pinto Pulley
meta: DMM Pinto spacer is a small accessory for the Pinto pulley that helps keep the carabiner and hitch lined up. A cheap fix for a tidier hitch climbing setup.
tagline: A small accessory that keeps your Pinto pulley setup aligned and tidy.
summary: The DMM Pinto spacer is a small accessory for the DMM Pinto pulley that holds the carabiner in position so the pulley and hitch stay lined up. It is a low-cost part that makes a hitch tending setup sit more neatly.
highlights: Accessory for the DMM Pinto pulley
Helps keep the carabiner positioned
Keeps the hitch and pulley aligned
Small, light and cheap
Check fit with your carabiner

p: The Pinto is one of the most common hitch tending pulleys because it has two attachment holes and a compact sheave. With a carabiner clipped through, though, the parts can shift and rotate as you climb, letting the pulley turn sideways to the hitch.

A spacer keeps things where they belong. The carabiner holds its position, the pulley stays square to the rope and the hitch feeds more consistently. It is a small upgrade, but many climbers notice the difference when tending slack on a long ascent.

It is also a cheap part to keep in the gear bag. Spacers are small and easy to lose during a system change, and having a spare means you can rebuild your hitch setup the same way every time instead of making do. If you run more than one Pinto, one spacer per pulley keeps both systems consistent.

Fit the spacer as DMM describes and make sure it does not interfere with the carabiner gate closing and locking fully. Check the whole assembly before each climb for wear, cracks or any part that has shifted.

The spacer is not a load-bearing connector. It does not replace any part of your life-support system, which should be used under ANSI Z133 practice and the maker's instructions by trained climbers. Find pulleys in micro pulleys.

faq.q: Does the spacer carry load?
faq.a: No. It positions parts. Load goes through the pulley and the carabiner as designed.

faq.q: Does it fit other pulleys?
faq.a: It is made for the DMM Pinto. Fit on other pulleys is not something to assume.

name: Petzl MOBILE Hitch Tending Pulley
title: Petzl MOBILE Pulley for Hitch Tending
h1: Petzl MOBILE Pulley for Hitch Tending
meta: The Petzl MOBILE pulley is a compact, light pulley that arborists use for hitch tending and quick redirects. Small enough to live on the saddle for every climb.
tagline: A small, light Petzl pulley that lives on the saddle for hitch tending and redirects.
summary: The Petzl MOBILE pulley is a compact, lightweight pulley with swinging side plates that arborists use for hitch tending and quick redirects. Its small size keeps a hitch system short and makes it easy to carry a spare.
highlights: Compact and light
Swinging side plates for easy rope installation
Good for hitch tending and small redirects
Easy to carry a spare
Check rope diameter range in Petzl's instructions

p: Clipped below your hitch, the MOBILE lets you pull slack through with one hand and keeps the hitch moving as you ascend. Because it is small, it keeps the distance between hitch and bridge short, so you lose less height on each advance.
It is also handy as a quick redirect pulley on a climbing line or for a small haul system, and it weighs little enough that many climbers carry one just in case.

The small size does come with limits. It is not meant for heavy loads or big haul systems, so keep it in its lane and carry a larger pulley for rigging and rescue jobs. For everyday hitch tending and light redirects, though, it is about as easy to carry as a pulley gets, and many climbers keep a second one on a gear loop for those jobs.

The swinging side plates let you put the pulley on the rope without unclipping everything. Make sure the plates close fully around the rope and that the carabiner is correctly placed through the attachment hole.

Inspect the sheave, axle and side plates before each use, and retire the pulley if it is cracked, deformed or stiff. Use it within Petzl's ratings and instructions and ANSI Z133 practice, and get trained before relying on it. Compare others in micro pulleys.

faq.q: Is the MOBILE strong enough for rigging?
faq.a: It is a compact pulley for light use. Heavy rigging needs a block rated for those loads.

faq.q: Can I use it with a hitch?
faq.a: Yes, hitch tending is one of its most common uses in tree climbing.

name: Petzl RESCUE Pulley
title: Petzl RESCUE Pulley: Prusik-Minding Pulley
meta: Petzl RESCUE pulley is a strong prusik-minding pulley with a ball bearing sheave, used by arborists for haul systems, rescue setups and loaded redirects.
tagline: A strong, efficient prusik-minding pulley for haul systems and redirects.
summary: The Petzl RESCUE pulley is a high-strength, prusik-minding pulley with a ball bearing sheave, built for hauling and rescue systems. Arborists use it for mechanical advantage setups, loaded redirects and aerial rescue kits.
highlights: Prusik-minding design
Ball bearing sheave for efficiency
Swinging side plates
Built for hauling and rescue loads
A staple of many aerial rescue kits

p: A prusik-minding pulley has square-cut side plates that stop a hitch from being pulled into the sheave. In a haul system, the progress-capture hitch sits against the pulley and holds the load when you stop pulling, so you can reset without losing ground.

That makes the RESCUE a good choice for tensioning lines, lifting a stuck piece in a mechanical advantage setup or building a system to lift or lower an injured climber. The ball bearing sheave keeps friction low so more of your effort goes into the load.

It is bigger and heavier than a hitch-tending pulley, so most climbers keep it in the rescue bag or rigging kit rather than on the saddle every day. That way it is ready for a planned haul or an aerial rescue without adding weight to every climb.
Match your rope diameter to Petzl's stated range and keep the pulley clean of sap and grit. Check that the side plates swing and close properly and that the sheave spins smoothly.

Rescue systems need practice. Train with your crew so you can build them quickly, and use the pulley within Petzl's ratings and ANSI Z133 practice. Inspect it before each use and retire it if it is cracked or deformed. See other pulleys in micro pulleys.

faq.q: Do I need a prusik-minding pulley for hitch climbing?
faq.a: Not usually. Smaller pulleys handle hitch tending. The RESCUE is aimed at haul and rescue systems.

faq.q: Is it heavy?
faq.a: It weighs about 370 g, which is more than a micro pulley but normal for a rescue-strength pulley.

name: Singing Tree Rope Wrench Pulley
title: Singing Tree Rope Wrench Pulley
meta: Singing Tree rope wrench pulley for SRS climbers running a Rope Wrench and hitch. Helps tend slack and keep the system moving on ascent and long limb walks.
tagline: A pulley for the Rope Wrench system that helps tend slack on single-rope climbs.
summary: The Singing Tree rope wrench pulley is made for climbers running the Singing Tree Rope Wrench on a stationary rope. It helps tend slack through the hitch and wrench so the system moves more smoothly on ascent and when working out on limbs.
highlights: Made for use with the Singing Tree Rope Wrench system
Helps tend slack on SRS climbs
Keeps the hitch and wrench moving together
From Singing Tree, the maker of the Rope Wrench
Confirm compatibility with your wrench and tether

body.h: How it fits the wrench system
p: The Rope Wrench adds friction above a climbing hitch so a hitch can work on a single, stationary rope. The hitch still needs tending, and a pulley below it lets you pull slack through with one hand as you move.

A pulley made for the same system is designed to work with the wrench and tether rather than fighting them. That keeps the setup compact and helps the wrench follow the hitch on ascent instead of hanging up.

Many climbers set up their wrench system once and leave it, so a matched pulley means fewer variables to manage. When it comes time to replace a part, staying with parts made for the system keeps the behavior you are used to. If you are new to the wrench, learn the system with an experienced climber before changing any part of it.

Follow Singing Tree's instructions for how the pulley, hitch, tether and wrench go together, and test the full system close to the ground before you climb. Small changes in hitch length or tether length change how the system behaves.

Inspect the pulley for cracks, grooves, deformation and a stiff sheave before each climb. SRS systems are life support, so use them within the maker's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice, and get trained first. See more options in micro pulleys.

faq.q: Do I need this pulley to use a Rope Wrench?
faq.a: No, but a tending pulley makes slack management easier. Many climbers use one.

faq.q: Will it work with other SRS devices?
faq.a: It is made for the Rope Wrench system. Check the maker's guidance before using it elsewhere.

name: SMC Crevasse Pulley
title: SMC Crevasse Pulley: Light Compact Pulley
meta: SMC Crevasse pulley is a light, compact pulley tree climbers use for hitch tending, redirects and simple haul setups. Easy to carry on the saddle every day.
tagline: A light, compact pulley for hitch tending, redirects and simple hauls.
summary: The SMC Crevasse pulley is a light, compact pulley originally aimed at mountaineering haul kits, and tree climbers use it for hitch tending, redirects and simple haul setups. It is small enough to carry on the saddle every day.
highlights: Light and compact
Good for hitch tending and redirects
Works in simple haul systems
Easy to carry as a spare
Made by SMC, a US hardware maker

p: A small pulley is one of the most useful pieces on the saddle. Under a hitch, it makes slack tending a one-hand job. On a redirect, it cuts friction and rope wear. In a simple haul, it helps tension a line or lift a small load.
The Crevasse is light enough that you will not mind carrying it. Many climbers keep one clipped as a spare for redirects even if they run another pulley for hitch tending.

It also makes sense in a small rescue or haul kit for the truck, where you want a few light pulleys that do not take up much space. When a rope gets hung up or a piece needs a quick lift, a light pulley and a few slings can save a lot of pulling by hand. Keep one with each rope bag and it will get used more often than you might expect.
Confirm the pulley fits your rope diameter and the carabiner you connect it with. Check that the side plates close fully and that the sheave turns freely without wobble.

Retire it if you see cracks, deep grooves or bent plates. Use it within SMC's ratings and instructions, and use life-support systems under ANSI Z133 practice after proper training. Browse more in micro pulleys.

faq.q: Is it strong enough for rigging?
faq.a: It is for light use. Heavy rigging needs a block rated for those forces.

faq.q: Can I use it for hitch tending?
faq.a: Yes, many climbers do. Check the fit with your hitch and carabiner.

name: ISC Aluminum Rings
title: ISC Aluminum Rings for Friction Savers and Slings
meta: ISC aluminum rings for building friction savers, adjustable anchors and sling setups. Light and smooth, sold in sizes so you can pair a large and small ring.
tagline: Light aluminum rings for friction savers, anchors and sling setups.
summary: ISC aluminum rings are light, smooth rings used to build friction savers, adjustable anchors and other sling setups in tree climbing. They come in sizes, so you can pair a large and small ring for a retrievable cambium saver.
highlights: Light aluminum construction
Smooth surface for rope to run on
Sold in sizes for large and small ring pairs
Common in DIY friction savers and anchors
Inspect for grooves and wear

p: Rings are the simplest hardware in a climbing kit. On a ring-and-ring friction saver, the climbing line runs through both rings so it does not rub on the bark, and the smaller ring passes through the larger one so the saver can be pulled down from the ground.
Rings also show up on adjustable anchors, as a connection point on a sling and in some rigging setups. Aluminum keeps them light, which matters when you are hauling a full kit up a tree.

Keeping a few spare rings in the gear bag is cheap insurance. When a sling or saver gets worn or you want to build a new anchor in the field, the hardware is there, and a ring that has started to groove can be swapped before it becomes a problem. Label or store spares so they do not get mixed with rigging hardware.
Pick sizes that suit the job: a big ring and a smaller one that passes through it for a retrievable saver. Check ISC's ratings for each size and use rings only within them.

Aluminum wears faster than steel under running rope. Inspect for grooves, sharp edges, cracks and corrosion before each climb, and retire any ring that shows wear. Use it in life-support systems only under ANSI Z133 practice and after training. See the full rings range.

faq.q: Aluminum or steel rings?
faq.a: Aluminum is lighter. Steel lasts longer under rope wear. Many climbers use aluminum for savers and steel where rope runs often.

faq.q: Can I use these for rigging?
faq.a: Use them only within ISC's ratings. Heavy rigging usually needs steel rings or blocks rated for those loads.

name: ISC Steel Rings
title: ISC Steel Rings for Climbing and Rigging Slings
meta: ISC steel rings for friction savers, anchor slings and rigging setups where rope runs often. Tougher than aluminum under wear, sold in several sizes for pairs.
tagline: Hard-wearing steel rings for savers, anchors and rigging where rope runs often.
summary: ISC steel rings are durable rings for friction savers, anchor slings and rigging setups where rope runs through them often. Steel resists grooving better than aluminum, so they last longer in high-wear spots.
highlights: Steel for better wear resistance
Good where rope runs often
Sold in sizes for paired setups
Used in friction savers and rigging slings
Heavier than aluminum

p: Every time a rope runs through a ring, it wears it a little. Aluminum grooves over time, and those grooves can end up sharp. Steel holds up much better, so it is a better choice for rings that see constant rope travel, such as on a friction saver used daily or a natural-crotch rigging setup.
The trade-off is weight. Steel rings are heavier, which matters less on the ground or for rigging than it does on a climber's saddle.

Steel rings also stand up better to the knocks of being thrown in a gear bag, dropped on a truck bed or dragged over bark. For rings that live in a rigging kit or on a friction saver that sees daily use, that toughness means fewer replacements over a season and less worry about sharp edges forming where the rope runs. Many crews keep a mix of sizes in the kit.

On a single-rope setup the rope hangs straight below you, so any spin goes straight into it. A swivel keeps that from turning into twists and knots in the tail, which makes the rope easier to manage and less likely to snag. The compact size also matters, since every extra inch between you and your device takes away from your reach on each advance and your comfort when working in position.
Make sure the carabiners on each side are correctly loaded and that the swivel turns smoothly under load. Keep it clean of grit and sap so the bearing stays free.

faq.q: Do they work with all Buckingham saddles?
faq.a: Not necessarily. Check Buckingham's compatibility for your model.

faq.q: Are they the same as a chest harness?
faq.a: No. Suspenders are mainly for carrying weight, while a chest harness is often built for SRS ascent.

name: Edelrid TreeRex Replacement Rope Bridge Kit
keyword: edelrid treerex replacement rope bridge kit
title: Edelrid TreeRex Replacement Rope Bridge Kit
h1: Edelrid TreeRex Replacement Rope Bridge Kit
meta: Edelrid TreeRex replacement rope bridge kit keeps your TreeRex saddle in service when the bridge wears. Know when to replace it and what to check first.
tagline: A replacement rope bridge for the Edelrid TreeRex saddle.
summary: The Edelrid TreeRex replacement rope bridge kit lets you swap a worn bridge on your TreeRex saddle. Bridges are wear parts, and a new one keeps the saddle working without replacing the whole thing.
highlights: Replacement bridge for the Edelrid TreeRex
Rope bridge kit
Keeps the saddle in service
Replace when worn
Follow Edelrid's fitting instructions

p: Your climbing system rides on the bridge all day. Sawdust, grit and constant movement wear it, so it is designed to be swapped long before the rest of the saddle.
Keep a spare kit in the truck so a worn bridge never puts the saddle out of service in the middle of a job.

A rope bridge also shows wear in ways that are easy to see if you look. Watch for fuzzing, flat spots, glazed patches from heat and stiffness where the connector rides most. Changing the bridge yourself is a good time to clean the saddle and look over the rest of it, including the attachment points the bridge runs through. Keep notes on how long each bridge lasts so you can plan the next one before you need it, and keep the old one out of the climbing kit so it is never mixed up with the new.
Fit the bridge exactly as Edelrid shows for the TreeRex and check any knots or connections before loading it. Hang on it near the ground before climbing.

Inspect the bridge before every climb for abrasion, glazing, cuts and stiffness, and replace it at the first sign of wear. Saddles are life support, so use one within the maker's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice, inspect it before every climb and get trained. See more saddle parts.

faq.q: Does it fit other Edelrid saddles?
faq.a: It is made for the TreeRex. Check with Edelrid before using it on another saddle.

faq.q: How often should I replace the bridge?
faq.a: Whenever inspection shows wear. Daily climbers may replace it often.

name: Petzl Seat for SEQUOIA and SEQUOIA SRT
title: Petzl Seat for SEQUOIA and SEQUOIA SRT
h1: Petzl Seat for SEQUOIA and SEQUOIA SRT
meta: Petzl seat for SEQUOIA and SEQUOIA SRT saddles adds support under your thighs for long stretches hanging in the tree. Read fitting and inspection tips here.
tagline: An add-on seat for Petzl SEQUOIA saddles for long stretches hanging in the tree.
summary: The Petzl seat for SEQUOIA and SEQUOIA SRT is an add-on seat that clips to those saddles and gives extra support under your thighs. It helps when you hang in one spot for a long time, such as a detailed pruning job or a long rigging setup.
highlights: Add-on seat for Petzl SEQUOIA and SEQUOIA SRT
Extra support under the thighs
Helps on long stationary work
Removable when not needed
Follow Petzl's fitting instructions

p: Leg straps carry your weight on narrow bands. After a long stretch hanging in one place, that pressure adds up. A seat spreads the weight across the backs of your thighs so you can stay put longer without losing circulation or focus.
That is useful on detailed pruning climbs, cabling and bracing work, or rigging where you spend time in one spot.

A seat is also a good fit for climbers who spend long stretches waiting in the canopy, such as during rigging operations where the ground crew needs time to clear wood between pieces. It does add a little bulk, so many climbers fit it on days they expect long stationary work and leave it off for quick pruning climbs. Store it with the saddle so it is ready when a long day comes up.
Attach the seat as Petzl shows for your SEQUOIA model and check that it does not interfere with the bridge, leg loops or gear loops.

Inspect the seat and its connections before every climb. It adds comfort but does not replace any part of the saddle. Saddles are life support, so use one within the maker's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice, inspect it before every climb and get trained. See more saddle parts.

faq.q: Does it fit other saddles?
faq.a: It is made for the Petzl SEQUOIA and SEQUOIA SRT.

faq.q: Can I remove it?
faq.a: Yes. You can leave it off on days you do not need it.

name: Petzl TOP CROLL Chest Harness
title: Petzl TOP CROLL Chest Harness with Ascender
meta: Petzl TOP CROLL chest harness with an integrated CROLL ventral ascender for single-rope ascent. Fits many arborist saddles to keep you upright on long climbs.
tagline: A chest harness with an integrated CROLL ascender for single-rope climbs.
summary: The Petzl TOP CROLL is a chest harness with an integrated CROLL ventral ascender, built for efficient single-rope ascent. Tree climbers add it to a saddle to keep upright and keep the rope close on long SRS climbs.
highlights: Chest harness with integrated CROLL ascender
For efficient single-rope ascent
Keeps you upright on long climbs
Fits many arborist saddles
Follow Petzl's fitting instructions

p: On a long single-rope ascent, a chest ascender keeps the rope tight to your body and lets you stand and sit with your legs doing the work. The TOP CROLL builds the CROLL into a chest harness, so it stays in the right place without extra parts.
Paired with a foot ascender or knee ascender system, it makes long, open climbs much less tiring.

The TOP CROLL is a common first step for climbers moving from footlocking or hitch climbing to a dedicated single-rope ascent system. It pairs well with a foot ascender and a knee or hand ascender, and many climbers add it to a saddle they already own. Check that it fits comfortably over the clothing you wear on the job and that it does not interfere with a saw lanyard or gear on your bridge. Practice converting from ascent to work mode low to the ground before you use it on a big climb.
Adjust it so the ascender sits close to your chest and the harness stays snug. Connect it to your saddle as Petzl describes, and practice the system low to the ground.

Inspect the ascender teeth, cam, frame and harness webbing before every climb, and retire it when worn. The ascender is only used for ascent, not as a work positioning device. Saddles are life support, so use one within the maker's instructions and ANSI Z133 practice, inspect it before every climb and get trained. See more saddle parts and shoulder harnesses.

faq.q: Do I need a TOP CROLL for SRS?
faq.a: No, but a chest ascender makes long ascents easier. Many climbers use one.

faq.q: Can I use it as my work device?
faq.a: No. It is for ascent. Switch to your work positioning device when you reach the work area.
